objectives: Distinguish sterilization, disinfection, and antisepsis and name the principal methods and agents for each.
Describe the sequence of surgical hand scrub, gowning, and gloving and articulate why each step matters microbiologically.
Apply the rules of the sterile field and the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist to real operative scenarios.

slides.title: Sterilization, disinfection, and antisepsis — a precise vocabulary
slides.body:
A cardinal error in operating room (OR) culture is treating sterilization, disinfection, and antisepsis as synonyms. They are not — each describes a distinct level of microbial kill, applied to different targets by different methods. Confusing them is not pedantic; it causes surgical site infections (SSIs).

**Definitions:**
- **Sterilization**: the complete destruction or removal of all viable microorganisms, including bacterial endospores. A sterilized object carries a **Sterility Assurance Level (SAL)** of \u2264 10\u207b\u2076 — a probability of one in a million that any viable organism remains. This is the standard for all instruments entering sterile body cavities.
- **Disinfection**: reduction of the number of pathogenic microorganisms on a surface to a level at which they do not pose a disease risk. Disinfection does NOT reliably kill endospores. High-level disinfection (e.g., glutaraldehyde) kills vegetative bacteria, mycobacteria, most viruses, and some spores. Intermediate and low-level disinfection target progressively fewer organism classes. Environmental surfaces in the OR — floors, walls, equipment — are disinfected, not sterilized.
- **Antisepsis**: application of an antiseptic agent to living tissue (skin, mucosa) to reduce the microbial load. The skin cannot be sterilized without destroying it, so antisepsis is the best achievable standard for patient skin preparation and surgical hand scrub.
- **Decontamination**: the process of rendering a contaminated item safe to handle — may combine cleaning, disinfection, and/or sterilization.

**Sterilization methods:**

1. **Steam sterilization (autoclaving)** — the workhorse of hospital central sterile supply. The autoclave was developed by **Charles Chamberland** (1851-1908), a collaborator of Louis Pasteur, who described the pressure steam sterilizer in **1879**. Steam under pressure raises the boiling point of water above 100 °C; standard parameters are **121 °C at 15 psi (103 kPa) for 15 minutes** (gravity cycle) or **134 °C at 30 psi for 3-4 minutes** (vacuum/pre-vacuum cycle). The killing mechanism is protein denaturation and hydrolysis. Biological indicators (Geobacillus stearothermophilus spore strips) confirm efficacy every cycle. Steam sterilization cannot be used for heat-sensitive items.

2. **Ethylene oxide (EtO) gas sterilization** — low-temperature process (37-63 °C) for heat- and moisture-sensitive items: flexible endoscopes, power tools, implants with electronics. EtO is an alkylating agent that disrupts DNA replication. Requires prolonged aeration after sterilization because EtO is toxic and carcinogenic. Cycle times are 10-16 hours including aeration.

3. **Hydrogen peroxide gas plasma** (e.g., STERRAD system) — low-temperature (50 °C), no toxic residues, cycle time ~28-75 minutes. Suitable for most heat-sensitive items except cellulose-based materials (paper, linens) and long narrow lumens.

4. **Gamma irradiation and electron beam** — used industrially for single-use devices (sutures, syringes, implants). Not practical in hospital settings.

5. **Dry heat** — higher temperatures required (160-170 °C for 1-2 hours) than steam because dry heat kills by oxidation rather than hydrolysis. Used for anhydrous oils, powders, and glassware.

**Antiseptic agents for skin preparation:**
- **Chlorhexidine gluconate (CHG)** — broad-spectrum, residual activity (binds to skin proteins and continues acting after application); active against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, some fungi. The agent of choice for surgical hand scrub (0.5-4 % solutions) and pre-operative skin preparation (2 % CHG in 70 % isopropyl alcohol, as in the **ChloraPrep** applicator).
- **Povidone-iodine (PVP-I)** — broad-spectrum including mycobacteria and viruses; does not have CHG's residual activity; inactivated by blood and organic matter. Available as aqueous solution (Betadine) or alcohol-based formulation.
- **Isopropyl and ethyl alcohol** — rapid kill, no residual activity, flammable. Require 30-second contact time for maximum effect. Used as vehicle for CHG and PVP-I in alcohol-based skin-prep products.
- **Quaternary ammonium compounds (quats)** — intermediate-level disinfectants for environmental surfaces; NOT appropriate for skin prep or instrument sterilization.

The distinction matters in practice: using a disinfectant on a surgical instrument, or an antiseptic intended for skin on an environmental surface, represents a category error with patient safety consequences.

slides.title: Surgical hand scrub, gowning, gloving, and the sterile field
slides.body:
The surgical hand scrub is the most ritualized activity in the OR, and the ritual exists for a reason. The goal is not to make the hands sterile — that is unachievable on living skin — but to reduce the resident and transient microbial load to the lowest achievable level, then maintain that reduction throughout the case using sterile gloves as a barrier.

**Hand flora — two populations:**
- **Transient flora**: organisms recently deposited on the skin surface from contact with patients, surfaces, or the environment. Predominantly Gram-negative bacilli and Staphylococcus aureus. Removed readily by washing and antisepsis.
- **Resident (normal) flora**: organisms that colonize the deeper layers of skin — hair follicles, sebaceous glands — and cannot be eliminated. Predominantly coagulase-negative staphylococci and diphtheroids. The significance: gloves perforate (the glove perforation rate in long operative cases exceeds 30 % in some studies), so these organisms constitute the true infective risk through glove failure.

**Surgical hand scrub — two accepted protocols:**
1. **Traditional timed scrub** (the Halsted legacy): 5-minute scrub with a chlorhexidine or PVP-I brush/sponge, beginning at the fingertips and working to the elbows. The first scrub of the day is 5 minutes; subsequent scrubs between cases may be 3 minutes. Hands are held higher than elbows throughout to prevent re-contamination by water running from the (less-scrubbed) proximal arm.
2. **Alcohol-based hand rub (ABHR) for surgical scrub** (WHO-endorsed since 2009): hands washed with soap and water first, dried, then ABHR (typically a 60-95 % alcohol formulation) rubbed over hands and forearms in a specified sequence until dry (~3 minutes). Non-inferior to traditional scrub in reducing bacterial counts; avoids skin damage from repeated brush scrubbing.

**Gowning sequence:**
1. Hands dried on a sterile towel (from the sterile gown pack), using one end for each hand.
2. Sterile gown donned with arms extended; circulating (non-sterile) nurse ties the back.
3. The front of the gown from chest to table level, and the sleeves, are considered sterile. The back of the gown is NOT sterile (cannot be seen or controlled by the wearer). The axillary region is NOT sterile.

**Gloving:**
- **Closed gloving technique**: hands remain inside the gown cuffs while gloves are donned; reduces the risk of contaminating the glove exterior with ungloved skin. Standard for initial gloving.
- **Open gloving technique**: used when re-gloving a single hand during a case.
- **Double gloving**: reduces the risk of glove perforation reaching the hand; endorsed by the WHO and required by many units for HIV-positive patients, long cases, and orthopedic implant surgery. Colorimetric double-glove systems (outer glove lighter than inner) allow detection of perforation by color change.

**Rules of the sterile field** — the operating principles every scrubbed team member must internalize:
1. Only sterile items touch sterile items. If sterility is in doubt, assume contamination.
2. Sterile persons and items contact only sterile areas; unsterile persons and items remain outside the sterile field.
3. Sterile drapes define the sterile field around the patient; the area below the level of the draped table is unsterile.
4. Sterile persons keep their hands within the sterile zone (above waist, below shoulder level, and in front of the body).
5. Movement around the sterile field is minimized; scrubbed persons pass back-to-back or face-to-face, never unsterile-person-to-sterile-person front-to-front.
6. Sterile fields must be maintained continuously — a momentarily unmonitored sterile field is a compromised sterile field.
7. Any item falling off the sterile field (or whose sterility cannot be confirmed) is unsterile.

**Laminar-flow theaters**: modern ORs for implant surgery (joint replacements, cardiac prostheses) use **laminar airflow** systems that push ultra-clean filtered air downward in a unidirectional column over the operative field, dramatically reducing particulate and bacterial counts in the operative zone. The concept was developed by **Sir John Charnley** (1911-1982) at Wrightington Hospital in the 1960s as part of his total hip replacement program; Charnley also introduced **clean-air enclosures** and body-exhaust suits to reduce SSI rates in joint replacement surgery from the then-unacceptable levels of 7-9 % toward under 1 %.

slides.title: Surgical site infection, prophylactic antibiotics, and the WHO Checklist
slides.body:
Despite all precautions, surgical site infection (SSI) remains the most common healthcare-associated infection and a leading cause of operative morbidity. SSI is defined by the **CDC/NHSN criteria** (National Healthcare Safety Network, a surveillance system of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) as infection occurring within 30 days of an operation (or within 90 days if an implant is in place) involving the incision or deeper tissues.

**SSI classification:**
- **Superficial incisional SSI**: involves only skin and subcutaneous tissue.
- **Deep incisional SSI**: involves deep soft tissues (fascia, muscle).
- **Organ/space SSI**: involves any part of the anatomy opened or manipulated during the operation, other than the incision itself (e.g., intra-abdominal abscess after colectomy).

**Wound classification** predicts SSI risk:
1. **Class I / Clean**: no infection, no breach of respiratory, GI, or GU tract. SSI rate ~1-2 %.
2. **Class II / Clean-contaminated**: controlled breach of a hollow viscus. SSI rate ~5-10 %.
3. **Class III / Contaminated**: major break in sterile technique, acute non-purulent inflammation. SSI rate ~15-20 %.
4. **Class IV / Dirty**: established infection present preoperatively. SSI rate ~40 %.

**Prophylactic antibiotics** — the evidence base and timing:
The critical insight, established by **Miles, Miles, and Burke** in experimental work published in 1957 and confirmed in clinical trials throughout the 1960s-1980s, is that prophylactic antibiotics must be present in tissue **at the time of incision** to prevent bacterial colonization of the wound. Administration after incision — even 30-60 minutes later — is largely ineffective. Current guidelines (endorsed by the **American College of Surgeons** and **Surgical Infection Society**) specify:
- Antibiotic administration **within 60 minutes before skin incision** (vancomycin and fluoroquinolones within 120 minutes due to longer infusion times).
- **Re-dosing every 2 half-lives** during prolonged operations (e.g., cefazolin re-dosed every 3-4 hours).
- **Discontinuation within 24 hours** postoperatively (48 hours for cardiac surgery); prolonged antibiotic courses beyond this increase resistance without further SSI reduction.
- Agent choice: **cefazolin** (first-generation cephalosporin) for most clean and clean-contaminated cases; tailored agents for bowel surgery, cardiac surgery, and penicillin-allergic patients.

**The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist** — arguably the most important single document in patient safety published this century:
In 2008, **Atul Gawande** (b. 1965), surgeon and Harvard professor, led a multicenter study across eight hospitals in eight countries under the WHO's **"Safe Surgery Saves Lives"** initiative. The resulting paper — **"A Surgical Safety Checklist to Reduce Morbidity and Mortality in a Global Population"** — was published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* in **January 2009**. The study found that implementing a 19-item checklist reduced the rate of death from 1.5 % to 0.8 % and inpatient complications from 11 % to 7 % across the study sites.

The checklist has three phases:
1. **Sign In** (before anesthesia induction): patient identity, site, consent, allergy, anesthesia machine and medication check, difficult airway/aspiration risk, blood loss risk.
2. **Time Out** (before skin incision): team introductions, patient identity/procedure/site confirmed aloud, antibiotic prophylaxis confirmed, anticipated critical steps, imaging displayed.
3. **Sign Out** (before the patient leaves the OR): counts confirmed (instruments, swabs, needles), specimen labeling, equipment problems reported, recovery/management concerns.

Gawande's book *The Checklist Manifesto* (2009) popularized the findings for a lay audience and catalyzed adoption in hospitals worldwide. The WHO checklist is now used in the majority of operating rooms in high-income countries and is increasingly implemented globally through the WHO's surgical safety programs.

**Joseph Lister's legacy**, then, is not merely carbolic acid spray — it is the entire intellectual architecture of asepsis: the idea that the surgeon's duty is to prevent contamination rather than to react to infection. From Lister's 1867 *Lancet* paper to Halsted's rubber gloves to Chamberland's autoclave to the WHO checklist, each step has been a refinement of the same foundational proposition: the microorganisms that kill patients can be controlled, and controlling them is the surgeon's responsibility.

question.question: Which of the following correctly defines sterilization and distinguishes it from high-level disinfection?
options: Sterilization kills all vegetative bacteria; high-level disinfection additionally kills endospores.

Sterilization achieves a Sterility Assurance Level (SAL) of \u2264 10\u207b\u2076 — complete destruction of all viable organisms including endospores, demonstrated by biological indicator testing (Geobacillus stearothermophilus for steam autoclaving). High-level disinfection kills vegetative bacteria, mycobacteria, most viruses, and some (but not all) spores — it does NOT reliably achieve SAL 10\u207b\u2076 and is therefore inappropriate for instruments entering sterile body cavities. The autoclave (steam sterilizer) was developed by Charles Chamberland in 1879 at Pasteur's institute and remains the gold standard for heat-stable surgical instruments.
Sterilization and high-level disinfection are functionally equivalent for surgical instruments that contact sterile tissue.
High-level disinfection achieves SAL 10\u207b\u2076 and is therefore equivalent to sterilization for most surgical purposes.
question.explanation: Sterilization achieves SAL \u2264 10\u207b\u2076 — a one-in-a-million probability of any viable organism remaining — including bacterial endospores. High-level disinfection does not reliably kill endospores and does not achieve SAL 10\u207b\u2076. All instruments entering sterile body cavities must be sterilized, not merely disinfected. The autoclave (Chamberland, 1879) is the reference method for heat-stable items.

hints: Think about endospores — which process reliably kills them?
slides.workedSolution: Sterilization = SAL \u2264 10\u207b\u2076, including endospores. High-level disinfection \u2260 sterilization — it kills most but not all organisms and is inappropriate for instruments entering the body. Charles Chamberland (1851-1908) developed the steam autoclave in 1879, still the gold standard for heat-stable surgical instruments.

question.question: The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist was validated in a landmark NEJM study. Which of the following correctly identifies the lead author, publication year, and the magnitude of mortality reduction observed?
options: Joseph Lister, 1867 Lancet; mortality reduced by 35 percentage points.
Peter Pronovost, 2006 NEJM; mortality reduced from 4.0 % to 0.0 % in ICU.

Atul Gawande, NEJM January 2009 ('A Surgical Safety Checklist to Reduce Morbidity and Mortality in a Global Population'); mortality reduced from 1.5 % to 0.8 % across eight hospitals in eight countries, with in-hospital complications falling from 11 % to 7 %.
Lucian Leape, 2001 IOM report 'Crossing the Quality Chasm'; mortality reduction not reported.
question.explanation: Atul Gawande led the WHO 'Safe Surgery Saves Lives' multicenter study published in NEJM in January 2009. The 19-item checklist, applied across eight hospitals in eight countries (rich and low-income), reduced mortality from 1.5 % to 0.8 % and inpatient complications from 11 % to 7 %. Peter Pronovost's 2006 NEJM paper addressed central-line infections in ICUs, not surgical safety.

hints: The lead author also wrote 'The Checklist Manifesto' (2009).
The study spanned 8 hospitals in 8 countries.
slides.workedSolution: Atul Gawande (b. 1965), NEJM January 2009. The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist reduced mortality from 1.5 % to 0.8 % and inpatient complications from 11 % to 7 % across eight diverse global hospitals. Gawande's 'The Checklist Manifesto' (2009) spread the findings to a wider audience.

question.question: Cefazolin has a half-life of approximately 1.8 hours in patients with normal renal function. Current guidelines recommend re-dosing every 2 half-lives during prolonged surgery. How many minutes after the initial dose should the first re-dose be administered? Round to the nearest whole minute.
question.hint: 2 half-lives = 2 × 1.8 h = 3.6 h. Convert to minutes: 3.6 × 60 = 216 minutes.

question.question: A breach of the sterile field during a right hemicolectomy
question.prompt: Forty-five minutes into an open right hemicolectomy for colon cancer, the scrub nurse notices that the circulating nurse — who is unsterile — has reached across the sterile instrument table to retrieve a fallen suture packet without announcing the breach. The scrub nurse informs the operating surgeon. Describe: (1) the immediate response including which items are now compromised and why; (2) the wound classification for this case before and after the breach; (3) what information should be communicated at the WHO Sign Out; and (4) whether prophylactic antibiotic re-dosing is affected. Reference the rules of the sterile field and the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist structure.

In \u2264 140 words, explain to a medical student observing their first operation why the surgeon scrubs for several minutes before gloving, and why double gloving is recommended. Reference resident versus transient flora, the Halsted legacy of rubber gloves, and one relevant statistic about glove perforation.
question.rubric: Should distinguish transient flora (removed by scrubbing) from resident flora (hair follicles, sebaceous glands — irreducible by antisepsis). Should explain that gloves fail — perforation rates exceed 30 % in long cases — so pre-gloving antisepsis protects the patient when gloves breach. Should connect rubber gloves to Halsted (c. 1890, Goodyear Rubber, Caroline Hampton). Should mention double gloving as an additional barrier and optionally note colorimetric glove systems for perforation detection. Bonus: reference WHO 2009 ABHR hand-rub protocol or chlorhexidine gluconate residual activity.
